tb21_profile.skill: Recover an exact discrete state (piece placement on an 8x8 grid) from a raster image, then search the legal-move space for every winning move and emit them in algebraic square notation
tb21_profile.domain: Image-to-structure extraction (pixels/OCR) plus board-game rules and engine-style search (chess, python-chess/stockfish)
tb21_profile.task_form: solve-a-puzzle end to end: perceive the input, compute the optimal answer, write all answers to a file in a strict format

searches: tools.py search all 'puzzle|solver|best move|optimal move|winning|N.?Queens|maze|game state'
tools.py search tmax 'backtracking|constraint satisfaction|branch and bound|optimal (solution|move|assignment)|exhaustive search|brute.?force'
tools.py search all 'steganograph|steghide|exiftool|zbar|decode the QR|hidden .{0,15}(in|inside) .{0,15}(image|photo|picture)|ASCII art'

notes: There is no chess, FEN, stockfish or checkmate anywhere in the 56k pool (searched all five corpora), so nothing matches end to end. I split the task into its two real demands - recover exact structure from a raster image, and search a board's move space for all winning answers - and ranked on those. TMax owns the first half (a large family of extract-the-graph-from-a-diagram-image tasks; I preferred the ones where the image encodes a spatial structure rather than a paragraph of settings). TerminalWorld and RTS own the second half via the N-Queens pair and the Sudoku/Prolog puzzles. SWE-Smith has nothing game-like at all: its ten are grid-coordinate parsing (gspread A1 notation), coordinate clustering (pdfplumber) and raster manipulation, honest 2-3s. SWE-Rebench at least has pelita (a bot game engine) and the axelrod strategy corpus, which is genuine choose-the-right-move code. The lexical shortlist was near-useless here - it returned graph-database and zinit Tic-Tac-Toe-build tasks (the latter share only the string 'Tic-Tac-Toe'; they are C build chores and I excluded all ~40 of them).
